items.body:
Tribal trance techno pioneers PWOG yield a 1st reissue of their debut album since ’93, replete with all tracks from the CD edition on vinyl. RIYL Zoviet*France, Muslimgauze, Mappa Mundi.

A real one for yoghurt weavers and armchair psychonauts, ‘Ov Biospheres And Sacred Grooves’ arrived in ’92 with a broadening and refinement of styles first spied on Psychick Warriors of Gaia’s propulsive, eponymous ’89 entry. Its maiden relaunch now christens Forever Records, a sub-division of Delsin focussed on classic album formats, with an exemplar of early ‘90s ambient techno LP interzones, surely paralleling the UK’s AI movement and characteristic of the way prevailing Euro DIY tape scenes - industrial, ambient, experimental - morphed into techno-trance and house mutations at the cusp of a new decade and era. 

The eight-track LP effectively contains the seeds of trance music as much as modern ambient club in its rangy drive between expansive, linear structures and turns toward downbeat and deep house, all of which were roughly part of the same, strange family during that pivotal period. Of course, the notion of “trance” would be codified, commercialised over the next decade, but in PWOG’s hands the sound is wide open and better defined by its sense of romance and an hypnotic immersion that patently endures for shine-eyed retro-futurists and those able to squint ears, hear the bridges between styles. 

A case in point is ‘The Challenge’, which best resembles their cult debut EP, but with a taut aerodynamic akin early Plastikman in Pt. I, but shores up in far trippier realms on a Pt. II that better reflects the rest of the LP. Between the sloshing tribalist rhythms of ‘Linkage’, the 11 min transition from nocturnal dread to buoyant 107BPM ambient house ‘The Tides (They Turn)’, or ultimate dip into warmest Balearic/Goan waters on ‘The Key (Version)’ and gently febrile ambient closer ‘New Edge Mantra’, they display how industrial, house, and ambient were all on the same page, with the same purpose that would be recognised by likeminded aerobic mystics who can join the dots.

items.body:
Steve Gurley and co.’s deeply inspirational run of ’92-’93 hardcore jungle 12”s are compiled into an ideal entry portal for budding junglists and ‘nuum surfers by the sound’s Bristol-via-Berlin torch carriers, Sneaker Social Club.

‘Origins’ contains some of the greatest music of the early ‘90s, particularly spotlighting the transition from rave’s rugged building blocks into artfully hi-tech dance music during a pivotal period. Sifting gems from both volumes of Foul Play’s early EPs on Oblivion Records - including the all-timers ‘Dubbing You’ and ‘Ricochet’ - plus an early 12” for Moving Shadow, the set documents breakbeat hardcore hitting a creative zenith of hyper-chopped soul, dub and pop samples arranged with staccato stabs, cut-up, shuffling breaks and drum machines, right in the pocket before it was codified as jungle. 

Thanks to the studio ingenuity of Steve Gurley, who cut his teeth on these recordings, the set can also be heard to characterise the development of what is known as the hardcore continuum, as defined in Gurley’s subsequent shift into jungle, proper, and then UKG - the ultimate refinement of hardcore’s 2-step shuffles and sexier swerve. The seeds of enduring styles & patterns to come are sown here, from he fractious rush of ‘Finest Illusion’ through the haunting zinger ‘Dubbing You’, to the needlepoint discipline of ‘Ricochet’ and effortless, toes-off-the-floor skip and parry of ‘Screwface’, to the jump-up jungle blueprint ‘Ragatere’.

items.body:
Hot on the heels of their ‘Junglist!’ set, Soul Jazz reload their anthem-studded 2007 comp, packing early-mid ‘90s hardcore and ragga jungle heat by M-Beat & General Levy, Ragga Twins, SUAD, Cutty Ranks x DJ SS.

‘Rumble In The Jungle’ tells the story of jungle’s rapid evolution from mutant hip hop x dancehall in the late ’80s, via hardcore, to its hugely distinctive ragga and jump-up phase of the mid ‘90s. It’s a baga sounds that successive waves of producers have attempted to emulate ever since, but simply doesn’t get better than the OG tackle, as Soul Jazz well know.

The Ragga Twins understandably dominate the set with three bullets, the foundational, acid dancehall rap of ‘Ragga Trip’, sped-up fast rap steez of ‘Illegal Gunshot’, both from 1990, plus the ragga techno of ‘Tan So Back’ (1992), which all sparks so many dances and imaginations BITD. Shut Up and Dance, who issued all the above, are also on board, but with the gummy 2000 garage of ‘No Doubt’, which is hardly a standard, but does show how the sound had muted 10 years later.

The rest is all dead solid as a primer for inquisitive junglists/junglettes, firing General Levy’s alternative national anthem ‘Incredible’ and the murderous DJ SS remix of Cutty Ranks’ ‘Limb By Limb’, beside lesser known but wicked zingers such as DJ massive’s clattering hardcore rufige in ‘Final Conflict’, a deep fried steppa by The Source, and of course X Project’s deadly ramp of Beenie Man & Barrington Levy’s ‘Under Mi Sensi’.

Finally following up 2019's cult tribal reconstrucción 'System', Delia Beatriz trades hauntology for rhythmic momentum on 'Potpourri', imagining a parallel timeline where guarachero evolved in conversation with acid house and dub techno, fusing its fundamental tresillo reticulations with caustic 303s, Chain Reaction-style echoes and ferocious psychedelic distortions. RIYL Dengue Dengue Dengue, Verraco, DJ Babatr, Safety Trance, British Murder Boys or Lechuga Zafiro

Beatriz has always balanced her dedication to the dancefloor with higher minded obsessions; even her debut album, 2018's NAAFI-released 'Animus', was a 50/50 split of rhythmic experiments and intoxicating soundscapes. But since combing the distant past on 2022's 'The Long Count' and her own musical autobiography on last year's cumbia rebajada love-letter 'Desaceleradas', the forward-thinking club hybrids that reached their peak on 'System' have taken a back seat. Thankfully, she picks up the trail on 'Potpourri', auditing her technique while simultaneously critiquing the past, present and future of Latin dance music. The conceptual rigor that anchored her last run of releases is intact, but 'Potpourri' is an album for the dancers, first and foremost, an arsenal of rave weapons that conspicuously straddles a conflicted border. Even the cover, surreptitiously shot on the bridge between the USA and Mexico, reflects the album's provenance, its grafting of genetic material sourced from Detroit, Chicago, Mexico City and Monterray.

'System' was an attempt to blend tribal guarachero with industrial techno and 'Potpourri' focuses the concept further, burying its roots deeper in techno's subsoil. Over an album length this time, Delia considers the fast-paced, non-linear way tribal legend Javier Estrada worked to redevelop her approach to writing club music from the ground up. "It's a manifesto for rethinking form and sound in dance music," she explains. "By stepping outside traditional structures and embracing the potpourri approach, I'm creating new meaning with familiar rhythms." We can hear exactly what that means on the cheekily-titled 'Assimilate', when familiar syncopated thuds plunge through a heaving mass of 303s, forming a compound that's part Jeff Mills, part Chico Sonido. But it's that high end that has us properly gripped; Beatriz knows that it ain't just kicks that'll infuse her potpourri so peppers in aromatic tresillo shakers, cutting almost to silence at the track's halfway point to make sure we fully comprehend the pyramid.

Similarly, on '2placesatonce', her corrupted hoover sounds and square wave bleeps are neatly offset with bass tangs and woody acoustic percussion, everything cooked in a layer of grizzled distortion. It helps, no doubt, that the album was mixed by Berlin-based club alchemist Ziúr, who waves her magic wand over the material and gives it the punch it needs to really dominate, whether it's on headphones or belting out of a full Function One setup. And that's completely necessary; just as 'Desaceleradas' was concerned with the feeling of nostalgia evoked from certain phrases or tonalities lifted from cumbia rebejada, 'Potpourri' is driven by the energy that runs through classic club records from both sides of the border. It's music that needs to be experienced on a physical level, inspired by potent memories and powered by Beatriz's desire to keep the contemporary scene evolving or, at the very least, searching.

Channel Zero, produced by the London-based Brazilian artist Protocol.

"Channel Zero is made up of 4 unprocessed live jam recordings of heavy, stripped-down techno. Composed over a period of 2 years, the artist focuses on experimenting on the far edges of techno, inspired by early avant-garde music, drone, and Musique Concrete.

Lost Signal (Noise) opens up the EP with reverberated static noise, followed up by a deep bass with more layers of percussion and atmospheric noise patterns, slowly evolving into unexpected rhythms. The second track, Blind Belief, is composed of a deconstructed kick sequence, with machinic-like sound structures in the background and a hi-hat that morphs with various envelopes, together with a nostalgic 909 rim-shot. Turning to the B side, Electromagnetic Shadow is an atmospheric four-to-the-floor techno track, where deep kick drums and polyrhythmic noise soundscapes move into industrial noise pattern. Closing Protocol's debut EP, Black Snow Cult brings together the EP's sound palette into aggressive patterns of Birmingham-esque industrial percussions, where synthetic sounds are put together in primitive sounding sequences together with high pitched frequencies."

items.body:
Sylvain Chauveau's first album since 2022's 'L'effet rebond', 'The Complexity of the Simple' is inspired by a Zen garden, a set of lovingly handcrafted minimal instrumentals that took 10 years to properly shape.

Chauveau was marveling at the lines drawn in the gravel of Kyoto's Tokaian temple when the idea for 'The Complexity of the Simple' appeared. He's been refining (and reducing) his sound for decades now - his last set was called 'Ultra-minimal' - but there's a different level of focus on display here, something controlled and, if not emotionless, then at least contemplative. By stripping away the fat of romance and aesthetic grandstanding from his earlier material, Chauveau has found a niche that's as peaceful and philosophically absorbing as that Zen garden. And, considering a future without fossil fuels and the producing, playing and listening that new era might provoke, he engages in a push and pull with sound that's engaging without being mawkish.

'Le Zen Dans L'Art Du Tir À L'Arc' transports us to Kyoto with its measured rhythmelodic chimes - from handpan, glockenspiel and synth - and on 'The Guitar Piece I Wrote for Masumi', Chauveau plays his instrument so softly that it almost evaporates. On 'Wabi Sabi for Beginners', he layers warbling synth tones on top of each other, creating beating rhythms that only appear if you're really tuning in, and on the final track 'Lignes Tranquilles Dans Le Gravier Blanc', he's joined by Tetuzi Akiyama on acoustic guitar and his longtime spar Cyril Secq, who follow his lead, playing lowercase notes into tempered radio interference and subtle, almost imperceptible environmental recordings.

items.body:
Berlin’s lowkey ambient wunderkind follows on the promise of his acclaimed albums since 2018 - solo and as half of OCA - plus production for Kelela, with a lush study in Vibroacoustic therapy intended to help his parents sleep better.

The hour long suite stems from Florian TM Zeisig’s rare visit to his parents’ gaff in rural Bavaria a few years ago, where he discovered they had been using a vibroacoustic mattress - a mattress kitted with transducers or speakers - to aid them in getting some quality kip. Being a good lad, Florian wanted to help his parents in their quest, and spent the next few years developing this soundtrack; a serene 60’ of music resting on a rich bed of layered sub-bass frequencies that surely beckon users to the horizontal. 

Most sensitively tending to this premise, Zeisig takes his role with requisite amounts of conceptual seriousness and gently witted pathos that have come to define his work, as on the critically acclaimed OCA album ‘Aging’ with Yo van Lenz in 2018, and in 2020’s deeply charming ‘Coatcheck’ soundtrack for cloakroom assistants. Working within the “vibroacoustic” framework, his results are typically gorgeous and user-friendly, playing into the space between new age ambient music’s putative therapeutic purposes and its well intended pseudo-science, with a warmly sublime conception of classic ambient music that beautifully resonates with records from Eno to Space Afrika and Midori Takada.

items.body:
Nuke Watch returns with a Fusion on Sagome, expanding into a trio formation with musician Zack Stafford on wind instruments and electronics, bringing together different strands of musical interaction and live experiences that occurred over 2024 in various legendary locations in and around NY,

"For the last 6 years, New York sampledelia and synthesis rhabdomants Nuke Watch, duo of Aaron Anderson and Chris Hontos, also known for alternative projects and spinoffs like Beat Detectives and Weird Shit U.S.A. 2, have consistently composed and released cerebral flows of psychedelic compositions bridging the gap between the post-hippy movement wastelands, the weirdest fringes of urban beatmaking subcultures, and the wild American DIY avant-garde and noise traditions for labels like The Trilogy Tapes, There (RVNG), Post Present Medium, Patience/Impatience.

Somehow inspired by the vertiginous technical virtuosity of musicians and projects like King Crimson, Tony Williams, and John McLaughlin, Fusion transposes the genre’s passion for impossible key changes and whimsical compositional complexity to the realm of free-form, instant composition, becoming a document of NW’s group jam sessions and the practice of collective improvisation. Scant overdubs.

Even if Nuke Watch ends up keeping the same key and pace for the majority of the album, there is the feeling that Fusion is a thematically apt title to describe how these artists stay with the music, finding a special space halfway between stimulation and observation: a methodical, trance-like process of waiting for music to plod along and morph over and over, endlessly. In this sense, “Fusion” is a simple way to describe combining different things to make something “new”; a quasi-alchemical process happening both at an atomic level and in the mind.

With their distinct imagery and tone, Nuke Watch channels millenarist stoner anxieties and end-of-world visions, expressing it through the distinctive contemporary psyop mystique of nuclear threats, dead new continents, and psychotic breakdowns. Enter a wormhole of laid-back, demented prophetic cultures and somewhat poetic hallucinatory paranoias through magic staircases, war locks, swarm of bees, wireless bamboos and Trip-free relays. Whether you are a neophyte or a long-time initiate to the “watch”, welcome to the Fusion."

items.body:
On their third album, Henry Birdsey's New England collective submerge windswept Americana in dense, oddly-tuned dronescapes, meditating on folk's origins and future eventualities by stirring banjo and slide guitar phrases with abyssal reeded wails and grungy tape loops.

Best known for his subterranean work with Zach Rowden as Tongue Depressor, Birdsey is one of the New England scene's most prolific operatives. 'Dissection Maps' comes only moments after last year's mossy 'Sewn the Name', and picks up where its predecessor left off. There's a different cast this time around (though how many of the contributors are Birdsey's pseudonyms we can't tell you), but the result is largely similar. Birdsey (or J.M. Eagle) plays banjo, pedal steel, bagpipes and resonator guitar, and takes the lead throughout, jangling over Ann Rowlis' organ, bells and rattles on opener 'Sleeps With Dice', the album's straightest nod to its roots. Things start to disintegrate on 'Singing Loom' when the discernible riffs are traded for magickal sustained tones that seem to melt into one another. It's not clear exactly what instrument is playing or when, but Addison Starkweather-Price's harmonica is a constant, and we're sure we can hear bagpipes in there somewhere.

Reana Doram steps in to add ghostly hammered dulcimer chimes to the gusty 'Dealt in Silver', playing against Grainger Farnsworth's doom-y electric bass punctuations and Rowlis's chilling organ and bells, and she shows up again on the mind-bending closer 'Last Rings', adding galloping rhythms to Ryder Tarbox's fluttering tape loops.

A second pressing of last year’s gorgeous fourth and final album from Old Saw, the American Primitive project of Tongue Depressor's Henry Birdsey, riffing on the classic Takoma paradigm with additional ferric washes and layered instrumental drones, huge recommendation if yr into Bruce Langhorne’s ‘The Hired Hand’ or classic work by Daniel Lanois, Laraaji, Pelt, Stars Of The Lid, State River Widening.

'The Wringing Cloth' is Birdsey’s fourth and final Old Saw outing, and ironically it’s also the one that has garnered most amount of critical and commercial success. Old Saw’s shimmering, drone-heavy soundscapes were recorded on 1/4" tape at various locations in New England over the last few years and are once again paired with evocative black and white imagery from photographer Dylan Hausthor, whose landscapes somehow perfectly capture the timeless, widescreen appeal of the music inside.

Birdsey's pedal, lap steel and resonator are at the core of each track, but the album also features Old Saw’s usual personnel; Harper Reed on nylon string guitar and banjo, Ira Dorset on fiddle and bowed strings, Ann Rowlis on reed organ and harmonium, Jim Cutler on telecaster, Addison Starkweather-Price on bass, and Peter Catchpole on metal objects and power hammer. That lap steel lends the music its stylistic anchor, taking us through decades of American folk before gently fraying at the edges. Birdsey's application of classical minimalism - the themes that surge through his work with Zach Rowden as Tongue Depressor - is still somehow present here, especially as the record pulls into its second side and the shimmering country-fied atmosphere is pierced with bell-like sounds, but the overall mood and flavour of the record is distinctly easy on the ear and timeless in its appeal.

As the label put it, “What has always been uncanny about this music is that it arrives in a state at once familiar and obscured, like a memory weighed down with sensory information but no identifying details to place it. The Wringing Cloth walks off further into that geographical dream without time or language, until it’s just a speck of light….”

items.body:
Sickest Dagbani dance-pop from northern Ghana, all produced by Mohamed “Ebony” Fuseini of Studio Simpa, and voiced by Dickson Gawani, Bala Zaaku, and Yaa Naara, among others - FFO DJ Tobzy, DJ Diaki, Nozinja, Music From Saharan WhatsApp

Issued on the Autotune The World label that shares its name with Chris Kirkley's long-running NTS show, ‘Digital Dance Music on VCD from Dagbon, Northern Ghana’ follows the show and label’s hyper-specific focus on the likes of Tecnobrega from Brasil and Caribbean Soca & Chutney with a rare jag upcountry in Ghana’s predominantly Muslim north. 

Armed with phone mic, FL Studio, and the best local singers on speed dial, Mohamed “Ebony” Fuseini updates local styles of Dagbani dance rhythm and melody with shiny VSTs and, of course, nuff autotune, to bring the rural sound closer to those from bigger cities, as heard on shared mp3s and physical media such as VCDs.

Available and traded at local markets, but rarely heard by international ears, those VCDs feature footage of women shaking hips - a “light cultural transgression” in the mostly Muslim area - with lyrics by local “Gawani”, flashy singers such as Dickson Gawani, Bala Zaaku, and Yaa Naara, with something to show, and matched by the energy of Ebony’s productions. Not as rushy as, say DJ Tobzy from Lagos, or DJ Diaki in Mali, Ebony’s Studio Simpa cuts are more melodic, pop-wise, maybe best compared with the colourful hi-energy of Shangaan Electro, heard on highlights from Dickson Gawani’s acidic percolator ‘So Tinha’ (also in a killer 12” bonus mix!), thru the lilting ballad ‘Baamunu’ by Obaako, to the unique skank of Aminu Dakogu, and the supremely light-headed effect of ‘M Be Adama’ by Alhassan Kukuonaa - all primed to light a fire on summer ’26 ‘floors.

items.body:
Japanese pianist Yumiko Morioka initially released Resonance, her first and only solo recording, on Akira Ito's ‘Green & Water’ imprint in 1987. Resonance has been lovingly remastered by Séance Centre's Brandon Hocura and given new artwork by Métron Records’ label head Jack Hardwicke.

"Recorded on a Bösendorfer grand piano, much of Resonance was made in an attempt to soothe her creative soul. Constructed from unwritten improvisations with additional instrumentation added later, Resonance explores the space between notes. As such, it's a record that feels open and inviting, permeated throughout with a sense of confident serenity.

The sparse, delicately played notes are allowed to reverberate and echo through the spaces between themselves, giving each track a feeling of both grandeur and intimacy. Like the great pioneers of classical and ambient music, there's a timelessness to Resonance - a comforting, familiar feeling, as if these melodies have always existed.

Resonance drew influence from the popular environmental music culture prevalent in Japan during the late 80s, but it was also heavily inspired by Western musicians such as the avant-garde Parisian composer Erik Satie. Listening today, it still feels fresh and pertinent; a warm, contemplative reflection of a travelled woman."

items.body:
FELT survey Copenhagen's contemporary jazz scene with RMC graduate Vincent Yuen Ruiz’s intimate and strikingly minimal rendition of stifled percussion, spacious piano and precise double bass work, tipped FFO of The Necks x Talk Talk, naturally.

Ruiz is a seasoned jazz player who's also nursed a parallel reputation as a post-rocker, formerly playing bass in Plaistow. And it's this knowledge of a world outside of jazz that gives 'Trio' its edge. It's not a post-rock record, by any means, but it's not pure jazz either - or at least, it doesn't sound as if it's confined by the aesthetic. The ensemble formed in 2019, but their last record together, 2021's 'Le seul salut que je connaisse', was recorded as a six-piece. Ruiz strips the sound to its bare bones on 'Trio', relying on unusual percussive sounds (provided by drummer Anders Vestergaard) to fill in some of the gaps. And although Rasmus Kjær takes a de facto lead roll on piano, it's the rhythm section, commanded by Ruiz on double bass, that makes 'Trio' so fascinating.

There's an almost meditative sense of calm to opener 'Choral', with Vestergaard's bowed cymbal tones providing a neat bed for Kjær's Bach and Ravel-inspired flourishes. The tension is only released when Ruiz's soft bass enters the frame, played somewhere between improvisation and composition, minimalism and decelerated chamber jazz. Just as he slimmed down his ensemble, Ruiz slims down the pieces themselves, condensing and distilling his ideas so the record never gets busy, or outstays its welcome. Just head to the  central piece 'Weaving', beautifully balancing its measured piano with Vestergaard's odd flurries of percussion that sometimes appear for just a second.

We can hear post-rock - particularly the variety that Talk Talk perfected - but our brains are also directed into filling in the gaps. 'Trio' is an album that lives and dies on its pauses, focusing on decaying notes and echoing rhythms in all their quiet beauty.

Following June's brilliant 'Rhythm Archives', Holy Tongue's Al Wootton continues his hot streak, landing on Sähkö with half an hour of hazed, immersive rhythmic experiments, tracking from vintage dub(step) to minimal techno and confidently striding thru percussive forms that echo from the Balkans to North Africa. RIYL Shackleton, Azu Tiwaline, Muslimgauze, T++, Deena Abdelwahed.

Ever since he dispatched with the Deadboy moniker a few years back and reached into dubbier, more percussive spaces, Wootton's been figuring out exactly where his dexterous productions fit in.He's been most at home on his own Trule imprint, operating at his own pace and shaping the aesthetics as he goes, and 'Rhythm Archives' felt like a mark in the sand, a record that matched his interest in vintage gear and classic production methods with his dedication to wide-eyed, punkish experimentation. 'CRUX', his first record for legendary Finnish label Sähkö, follows that lead, assembling four long percussive jams that sound as if they've toppled off the timeline - if someone told us it was material rescued from a forgotten reel-to-reel, we'd believe it.

There's an outline of dubstep visible in the background on opener 'Essene' that's enhanced by the Skull Disco-esque sub-undulations and wormhole-splitting tape echoes, but the hollow hand drum runs and hallucinatory effects shuttle the composition into darker, more reflective landscapes. Similarly, the busted drum machine intro of 'Per Incanto' might reference Sähkö royalty Mika Vainio and Hertsi, but the track veers leftwards, muddling the mix with psychedelic African Head Charge-style reverberations and trapped, timestretched string loops. It's gear that's intended for deep, intentional listening; the tracks don't contain too much melodic content by design - Wootton's rhythms are layered and hypnotic, and anything else is there to reinforce the general spirit.

Just check 'Cloister', the EP's low-key stand-out, where the lead line is literally just tuned feedback, placed to disorient even the most abstinent listener, or 'Armen', that distorts its sputtering Bruce Haack-in-dub atmosphere with ghosted groans and faint remnants of a trip-hop undercurrent that never fully reached optimal pressure. If you've ingested all the psilocybin from Shackleton's recent run, this is yr next drop.

items.body:
The craziest label in Detroit back with another genius, unfathomable dose of destroyed Techno x Trip Metal, caked in Motor City crud and located on the factory line somewhere between Urban Tribe, H-Fusion and Wolf Eyes​

Seven years on from his debut ‘Bloodsport’, secretive 313 artist K-6000 only jags deeper into Detroit’s scuzzy underbelly on the rough hewn rhythmic noise and atmospheric trip metal of ‘War Games’. The 6-part album surely evokes the dystopia of modern Detroit’s knackered architecture in its cranky tone and offbeat structure, but also signals the underlying soul of its entities, and the lost futures they live thru, in its textured play of psyched sax and guitar spectres meshed with sampledelic tapestry of disembodied voices. 

A record that leaves dirt under yr nails, it unfurls at its own steady pace from free jazz noise like some Wolf Eyes re-score of Robocop, into grouchy bouts of squashed beatdown psych with ruggedest drum programming comparable to KDJ, Shake and Sherard Ingram’s chops with Kemetrix on the Urban Tribe album. It descends into the sleaziest mire of Blind Pig biker bar blooz, like Captain Beefheart jamming with H-Fusion, around the mid-section, and ultimately buckles into PCP-spiked industrial funk sludge in the final stages. 

Manna for sci-fi free jazz trip metal beatdown hounds, then!

items.body:
An extra sugary batch of queer cult pop fancies on Cairo’s ever-wonderful Nashazphone label; super melodic, passionate synth-pop songs about boys, beauty and the melancholy of youth, tipped for fans of Elli et Jacno, Taxi Girl and Mathematiques Modernes.

‘Hélas’ collects 15 songs from the repertoire of Neoboris, an infamous Bordeaux/Pau duo highly active in the late ‘90s and early ‘00s. Drawing on direct Punk, Wave, Rave Culture and “Variété Française” influences, it functions as a perfect time capsule of a very specific era and mood: a boy-and-girl duo celebrating their love for boys, with melancholy and beauty.

"The origin story reads like an archetype, but the details make it sting. One half of Neoboris came out of hardcore raves and Bordeaux punk bands, carrying the raw‑throated urgency of that milieu; the other, Boris, grew up on New Wave and goth, a born songwriter whose melancholic streak ran as deep as his knack for hooks. Together they found a common altar in Elli et Jacno, Taxi Girl, Mathématiques Modernes – that peculiarly French intersection where cheap drum machines, fragile synth lines and deadpan vocals can suddenly break your heart. Out of that devotion came a duo aesthetic: compact songs, simple structures, lyrics that flirt with kitsch and then side‑step into something sharper, all delivered with the kind of chemistry you can’t rehearse into existence.

Their shows were wild in the way that only under‑funded, over‑feeling gigs can be: feedback squeal, rushed tempos, voices occasionally cracking, the two of them radiating that mix of shyness and bravado you get when you’re singing your secrets out loud. Hélas gathers the studio and home‑recorded echoes of that era and orders them into an emotional arc – from rush to comedown, infatuation to regret, celebration to elegy. The production sits right on the fault line between DIY and pop: drum machines slightly out of time, synth presets pushed into unexpected shapes, guitars toggling between brittle and blissed, all wrapped around melodies that would sound just as right on a transistor radio as in a squat.

The shadow that hangs over the record is Boris’s death in 2008, a break so abrupt it turned the entire project into unfinished business. The surviving member’s decision to keep singing these songs “everywhere I can” isn’t nostalgia, it’s a refusal to let that voice vanish into footnote status. Hélas makes that refusal tangible: 15 tracks that re‑situate Neoboris not as local cult trivia but as part of a larger, messy history of queer‑coded, under‑the‑radar French pop. You hear the mourning in the title, of course, but the music itself leans hard into joy – messy, melancholy, shoulder‑to‑shoulder joy, the kind you find on cramped dance floors at four in the morning. Singing with him then, now, and forever: Hélas documents that promise in all its scruffy, luminous detail."

items.body:
Oh man, quite possibly the oddest, cutest thing we’ve heard this year - cult Japanese underground duo Tenniscoats sing and play over a bunch of iconic hip-hop and r'n'b instrumentals on an hour-long tape for A Colourful Storm’s choice Fleetway Tapes sublabel; a concept that’s so brilliantly wtf that we were sold before they even droped a beat.

Saya and Takashi Ueno have never confined themselves to a single genre over the years, bending softer-than-soft whimsical folk, indie pop and psych rock into their own unique shapes - but we still could never have imagined them produce anything like this. We can't tell you how Moopie managed to convince them to yank it from the archives, but it's a total joy - the most eccentric record in Tenniscoats' already distinctive catalogue. 

There's a level of warm fuzz that emphasises the mix was beamed in from another decade - the tape crackles to life with melodica wails that hang remarkably well over the sturdy, bass-heavy instrumental from Mobb Deep's 'Quiet Storm', the lead single from the foundational duo's misunderstood fourth album 'Murda Muzik'. It isn't an obvious track ('Temperature's Rising' or 'Shook Ones, Pt. II' would have been the casual's choice), but it's a stone-cold killer, boasting some of Havoc's dirtiest bass and a snare that could cut glass. Saya does her best to ad-lib her own rap at first, eventually settling into a sort of soft-hued spoken word that floats Havoc's beat from the Queensbridge projects all the way to Tokyo. 

Their take on TLC's 'No Scrubs' is even weirder, with Saya's fragile vocal turn and Takashi's fittingly flamenco-inspired acoustic guitar pushing the overfamiliar beat gently into new territory. You could say 'Hip Hop Tennis' is a karaoke mixtape of sorts, the kind of selection of hastily-made reworks and versions that used to litter the streets outside Brooklyn's Broadway Junction or down on the Lower East Side before the coffeeshops and Cronut stores moved in. But Saya and Takashi's impromptu jams elevate this into the sublime, as if they'd put together a mix of East Coast favourites in the early '00s and spontaneously added their own ingredients on top. Just check the duo's dubbed-out rhymes over Brand Nubian's 'Word Is Bond' or Saya's loungey turn on the underrated Neptunes-produced banger 'Light Your Ass on Fire' and you’ll know exactly what we’re saying.

It's a session that's brimming with a palpable affection for its influences; the first side ends with a lengthy half-speed Nuyorican love-in, and then the second bursts open with an uncharacteristically nursery rhyme-like flip of The Inc's low-key Ashanti-starrer 'No One Does It Better'. Saya's blustery, saturated wails even transform Eve's enduringly popular Dre-produced 'Let Me Blow Ya Mind', while Takeshi attempts to sand down the edges of DMX's 'X Gon' Give It To Ya'. But the best moment comes when Takeshi plays in a minor key over Jeru the Damaja's 'Come Clean' - probably the best East Coast hip-hop track of the '90s - completely re-contextualising it, and trust when we say we thought we'd heard every which way that track could be flipped. 

Even if you've been following Tenniscoats since 2000's 'The Theme of Tenniscoats' - you ain't ever heard them like this.

items.body:
Ezekiel Honig's glitchy, concréte house breakout, that originally surfaced nearly two decades ago, finally gets a new lease of life (and a fresh mastering job) thanks to the Keplar imprint.

Back in 2008, the world was already over microhouse. The glitchy, short-lived micro-genre had burned bright for a short moment; Philip Sherburne had coined the term in 2001 and by the time Akufen's 'My Way' had emerged just a year later it felt as if the shine had gone. Honig's 'Surfaces of a Broken Marching Band' arrived in 2008 and sounded like reformed traces of the recent past. The backbone was 4/4, crawling towards a slinky 120BPM minimal house, but the emotional content was completely different. This wasn't material that was aimed at the club or even the afterparty, it was loose, faded gear that Honig had made from meticulously collected foley sounds and environmental recordings - domestic elements that Matthew Herbert would be proud of.

And because the music slipped quietly into its own nook, it still sounds unique now, a record that deserves to be filed alongside Farben's early 12"s and Kit Clayton's iconic 'Nek Sanalet', even Ricardo Villalobos's primo gear - just peep the title track and tell us it doesn't sound like 'Easy Lee' made with a broken shortwave radio and a pinball table. Needless to say, if you're into Mark Templeton (who incidentally appears twice on this record) or the soon-to-be-hauntological Y2K aesthetic, you'll need to grab it without delay.

items.body:
An almost forgotten but bona fide Ambient classic floats up on this edition with the legendary Glasgow-based Ampoule label, newly remastered with a bonus cut for added immersion - highly recommended to fans of BoC, Balil, Porter Ricks.

Still every bit as woozy and gouched-out as we remember, Pub’s gingerly wistful debut album ‘Do You Ever Regret Pantomime?’ is a cult classc for those that know; a sublime example of a peculiar sound at its sensitive best. Back in 2001 it saw lots of rotation at our auld shop Pelicanneck and has since become prized for its effervescent melodies and light-touch drum programming that acknowledged and parsed influence from then-contemporary hip hop and post-rock as much as the prevailing trends of ambient and minimal techno. 

A plangent, elusive sense of nostalgia that arguably prefigures modes of hauntology beautifully percolates the album, dwelling on a melancholy state of mind that, with hindsight, speaks to a timeless sort of wistfulness and tentative tension surrounding the early years of the millennium. The tracks are perhaps detectably burred with a gently rolling accent and crepuscular glow that we’d attribute to Pub’s Scottish provenance and which clearly resonates with BoC, so it’s maybe best to play this album after theirs, when its vaporised textures and thizzing melodic tendrils will best work their exceedingly subtle yet palpable magic. 

The real deal this one.

items.body:
A gorgeous, properly influential ambient drift classic resurfaces complete with a new extended piece evoking gauzy nostalgia for late ‘90s/early ‘00s styles.

The glimmering iridescent dub electronics of’Summer’ bobs up from 2000 in the wake of a reissue for the reclusive Scottish artist’s lush debut album  ‘Do You Ever Regret Pantomime?’ (2001). There’s a legion of people out there for whom this was really one of the most definitive and influential records of the era, originally surfacing via Vertical Form and creating a sort of bridge between the foundational Chain Reaction template and the wave of atmospheric, Detroit-indebted UK Techno typified by the Likemind label, Stasis, Irdial etc. 

Newly remastered to taste, the original stretches out to the horizon with a groove and lilt that feels something like a re-wired take on ‘E2-E4’ overseen by Mark Fell and Terre Thaemlitz. It’s just inarguably lush, uplifting gear.

‘Fragile Root’ is exclusive to this release, and, although we’re not sure if it’s new-new, or old-new; either way it’s a perfect example of Ambient sculpting at its slinky and melancholic best, strongly recalling Plaid’s ‘Anything’ (the best ever Plaid track, right?) as well as the new wave of UK based producers at the time orbiting around labels like DeFocus, Headspace etc. A throwback - but weirdly a strongly comforting one.

items.body:
Returning to Hive Mind, Lebanese artist Yara Asmar collages reel-to-reel recordings of her family in Beirut with surreal cinematic interjections and textures extracted from her arsenal of toy instruments, metallophones and homemade music boxes.

If there's one thing that stood out about Asmar's excellent last Hive Mind offering 'synth waltzes & accordion laments', it was the storytelling. A puppeteer, Asmar's used to arranging her art into narrative segments, and pulls us further into her world on 'everyone i love is sleeping...', cutting her playful Švankmajer-esque chimes and resonances with ferric memories that edge us precariously towards war. Now based in upstate New York, she remembers Beirut not with nostalgia; "there is no future to yearn for and the past does not exist," she explains. It's a story about Asmar's isolated present that tells us who she is, via ghostly echoes and instruments weighed down with cultural baggage.

Asmar acknowledges the implications of using music boxes and toys, complaining that they're "burdened with sentimentality", so it's fascinating to hear her deal with this head on. Unlike her previous albums, that treated the instruments with a level of reverence, there's a purposeful disregard for order here that keeps things interesting. At their most affecting, her soundscapes are built from instruments abused, rather than used; chimes that ring through the album's early tracks distorted until they're sawed resonances on 'of the always puzzle...', and her music boxes sound like a doomed gamelan orchestra on the brief but satisfying 'for now we leave...'.

Asmar leads us through childhood, with twanging languid melodies on 'there are glorious labyrinths...' to genuine memories of home, ending with the resonant 'sounds from home', a set of powdery environmental recordings that she overlays with accordion and dissociated noise.

items.body:
In spring 2025, Abul Mogard and Rafael Anton Irisarri created the source material for their second album, Where Light Pauses in the Silence of the Sun, during a three-day residency at Morphine Raum in Berlin.

"Functioning as both recording studio and performance venue, the space has no stage, with the audience gathered around the performers. Working within an open framework, the duo reshaped the music each evening while recording the performances live to multitrack. Rotary speakers, modular synthesizers and bowed guitar formed the core of their sonic language, captured through a 1970s mixing console and microphones placed around the room.

Back in Mogard’s studio in Rome, the material was further crafted as motifs were stretched, fragments isolated, and tempos dissolved. Irisarri recorded additional guitar textures and treatments in New York, while passages recorded by Martina Bertoni and Andrea Burelli in Berlin reinforced the harmonic centres and brought breath, refinement and a new sensibility to their compositions. The process continued as Mogard’s layering and subtraction reassembled everyone’s parts into the final arrangement.

The album opens with “In the Eastern Wild,” building from a sparse outline into a monumental formation of low-frequency weight, its internal motion shaped by the rotating Leslie speaker. “Over the Domes” widens into a broader acoustic field, where sustained modular tones meet waves of softly plucked guitar. The music then turns inward with “A Blue Descent,” centred on Bertoni’s cello, whose growling timbre introduces a melancholic depth.

At the album’s centre, “In a Quiet Radiance” unfolds around a slow guitar ostinato, its luminous stillness opening into a more expansive and reflective state. Across its ten-minute span, Burelli’s violin lines and Bertoni’s lower cello phrases gradually surface, weaving through the harmonic field. Mogard brings Burelli’s processed voice to the fore, its emotive, operatic presence becoming one of the record’s pivotal moments. “Of Blessed Ages” suspends the sonic flow, shifting between parallel major and minor chords as lingering, slowly decaying melodies shape the music’s internal drift. The closing “Among Shadows” settles into a darker resonance as layered textures recede.

Mogard and Irisarri’s shared language balances restraint and maximalism. UK magazine Crack describes the music as “a tidal wave held in suspension,” while Dutch newspaper de Volkskrant writes, “What a colossal sound, and how this music strikes at the emotions.” Reflecting on the residency sessions, Irisarri recalls: “At moments I genuinely couldn’t tell if a sound was coming from me or from Abul. It stopped feeling like two people making decisions and began to feel like we were inside a system moving on its own."

Marja de Sanctis’ cover artwork revisits the vessel sculpture from the duo’s first album, Impossibly Distant, Impossibly Close. There it appeared as raw, unfired clay. Here it has been fired in the kiln and finished with a glaze. Light gathers on its polished surface and spills into the surrounding space. As she explains, “I wanted to convey the idea of continuity within the duo, and the vessel became a kind of container for that idea. However, their music felt different this time, and with the collaboration of Martina and Andrea, I felt it should have a sleeker, softer, more glamorous look, very distant from the first raw appearance.” The transformation of the vessel from raw clay to fired form suggests a passage from immediacy toward permanence, mirroring the music’s gradual expansion."

Italian club shapeshifter Piezo pulls from a native history of cosmic disco, trance and electronica on a diverse handful of aces nodding to Beppe Loda, Marco Passarani and Donato Dozzy.

Named for the Tibetan funerary rite, ‘Sky Burial’ follows in a guess-again run of dub, hard drum, and breaks-driven works of the past decade to portray Piezo at full dancefloor wingspan. They’re all fine-tuned for effortless motion, from a sleek title tune that spotlights how synth-pop paved the way for trance - think Chris & Cosey-meets-Pet Shop Boys - thru the urgently uptempo yet elegant electronica of ‘Their Amnesiac Colours’ harking late ‘90s Pssarani via Orbital, and the D’Arcangelo-type braindance of ‘Vimelodica’, next to something like Beppe Loda meets Black Merlin on ‘Bardo Climax’, and echoes of Donato Dozzy’s take on modern Roman trance in ‘Trunks’.

Last seen on vinyl in 1990, Clock DVA’s scuzzy blast of noirish skronk, spangled psych and cold war spy funk for Throbbing Gristle’s Industrial Records remains a wicked relic of a pivotal 1980 and exemplary of Adi Newton’s expansive vision - RIYL James Chance & The Controtions, Suicide, Cabaret Voltaire.

‘White Souls In Black Suits’ was recorded by an early iteration of CDVA led by an Adi Newton who a few years earlier had departed The Future, a prototype of The Human League, and was beginning to embark one of late C.20th electronic music’s most fascinating projects. The eight-part album captures Newton (voice, synth, clarinet, bowed electric guitar, and tape treatment) blaring beside Clock DVA co-founders Steven James Turner, David J. Hammond, Charlie Collins, Roger Quail, and Simon M. Elliott-Kemp, with Cabaret Voltaire’s Steven Mallinder & Richard H. Kirk overseeing from the studio booth at their Western Works Studio. Aye, lad, it’s a proper Sheffield thing, like vinegar buns, cutlery and inclines.

At the fore Adi Newton’s vox channels a troubled soul of late ‘60s garage psych and late ‘70s goth and industrial qualities, comparable to Gen P-O as much as Takashi Mizutani and Peter Murphy, but with his own prowling, scowling swagger binding their songs, stepping from th clipped cold wave funk of ‘Consent’ and fuzzed up sleaze of ‘Discontentment (1 & 2)’, thru 10 mins of lysergic, strung-out psych mumble and caterwaul on ‘Non’. They hit a needling, wiry ace with ‘Relentless’, and sow seeds for CDVA’ oddest tangents and fascinations with “surveillance, obsession, and psychological decay” with the soundscapes of ‘(Film Soundtrack Keyboards Assemble Themselves at Dawn)’ and atonal collage ‘Anti-Chance’.

Drums and jaw harp (Hans) meet modular synth and double bass (Egil) on Unit of Time.

"Hans Hulbækmo and Egil Kalman have long been a playful and creative rhythm section, with one foot in free jazz and the other in folk music. They’ve played together in the Marthe Lea Band and other projects, and since last year they’ve delved into the folk music of Norway and Sweden — all set in an experimental duo format.

Unit of Time draws from the rhythmic details of folk music, as the basis for minimalist compositions full of improvisation. It’s not all about the groove, though. Some melodies are interpreted straightforwardly enough, but the unconventional instruments give the music a new depth. Unusual timbres and sonic phenomena emerge, mesemerizing."

New from Gi Gi on Mood Hut - dubwise sampledelia​, written between Texas and Australia.

"Gi Gi describes his process as “dubwise sampledelia.” It begins with fragments and ends somewhere else entirely, destabilizing its source material until it stops pointing backward. A borrowed sound, looped and bent, eventually forgets where it came from; it stops referencing anything but itself.

This liquid sensibility shaped his earlier work, music that hovered between drift and propulsion, suggesting the dance floor without fully stepping onto it. Presence was implied, edges stayed soft. The center was always there, but diffused like mist on a screen.

With In Lieu, that center comes into focus. Half written in Texas, half in Australia, the shift isn’t simply geographic, but internal. The record moves with a coiled, anticipatory energy; the drums arrive with more force and the bass organizes the room instead of melting into it. It's dense with the feeling of more bodies in the frame. Textures still smear and refract, but they move around a clearer axis. 

Where past records circled their core, these inhabit it, pulling closer to the body. “Some Of” and “Arque” lean into low-end pressure without abandoning his instinct for drift. "Pink Dirt" circles around mechanical drums and dizzying vocal chops, head-down and visceral.  Elsewhere, voices gain newfound contour, materializing in “Downswept” with intimate musings and nearly forming a lead vocal on the title track before dissolving again.

In Lieu moves with a newfound confidence, compressing inward, sounding closer to the source of its own pulse."

Landmark, evergreen debut by the eternally charming singer-songwriter, ushering bossa into the emerging tropicália sound in ’67, on a round of songs laced with a political bent that would see him and Caetano Veloso locked up by the military regime in ’69...​

"Arriving on the eve of Tropicalismo, the record places Gil’s guitar at the center of rich arrangements by Carlos Monteiro de Souza, Dori Caymmi, and Leonardo Bruno. Blending samba, bossa nova, carnival traditions, and Northeastern Brazilian rhythms, the album explores social, political, and religious themes. The title track “Louvação,” co-written with Torquato Neto, calls for collective awareness, while “A Rua” carries a bittersweet nostalgic tone. Gil’s deep connection to Bahia flows through “Beira-Mar” (with Caetano Veloso), and his poetic imagination shines in “Lunik 9,” reflecting on the space race. “Ensaio Geral” captures the political energy of carnival, while “Rancho da Rosa Encarnada” (with Torquato Neto and Geraldo Vandré) evokes traditional festivities. Highlights include the rhythmically inventive “Roda,” the celebratory “Viramundo” (with Capinan), and the nostalgic “Água de Meninos.” The romantic “Maria (Me Perdoe, Maria)” offers a moment of intimacy, while “Procissão” closes the album with a powerful reflection on faith and society."

Hashman Deejay mints a new alias with a ruck of curdled circuitry, hardcore jungle tekno and downbeats acutely advised FFO Rezzett, Demdike Stare, Jega, Ragga Twins, 2 Bad Mice.

A longtime regular on Future Times and Mood Hut, and also known as half of Aquarian Foundation, Tanner Matt really flexes a ruffer range on Newroomfreak’s eponymous debut. Aside to a pair of gunky beat-less and beatdown works, its all about the full bore rave pressure here, authentically emulating a heyday of ’92-’93 breakbeat hardcore with the brutal body animator ‘Newroomfreak [WIDE]’ calling to mind the Amiga-squashed breaks of early Chaos & Julia Set via Jega’s Skam gems, whereas ’40z’ gets looser, splashier with the breaks in widescreen mode, where his ‘New Out’ wriggles for 10 mins of tail-chasing breaks and flyaway flute licks to get teeth and feet gnashing at the bit.

"Striking the sweet spot between sampledelic downtempo and earth-rooted deep house, Fila Brazillia’s Old Codes New Chaos is a maverick patchwork of grooves and soundscapes crafted in North East England, a cult classic suite spanning deep house, broken beat and ambient shot through with wry humour.

Forever Records is a reissue series dedicated to rediscovering lost musical treasures from across the spectrum of head-feeding, heart-rending electronic music.. Established by Rush Hour co-founder Christiaan Macdonald and Delsin founder Marsel van der Wielen."

items.body:
A wealth of DIY dubplates and 45s from Jah Massagan’s East London sound crop up for first time on tape with cherry-picking label Death Is Not The End - heavy roots dub troubles cut at the studios of King Tubby, Lee Perry, Channel One, and Joe Gibbs…

Eljay Mass, son of Jah Massagan’s owner-operator, Lloyd Mass, dips into his dad’s enviable archive for an hour of rare, one-away platters that hail a self-organising rhizome of sound systems which sprang up in the UK with arrival of the Windrush generation, and brilliantly altered the course of music on this strange island in the process. 

The cassette-only session speaks to prevailing links between Caribbean culture and UK inner cities which reverberated from the ‘70s into the ‘80s, and has endured as a touchstone for some of our isles’ most vital music, setting templates for independent distribution networks and producing waves of innovative hybridisation.

Owner-operator Lloyd Mass and his childhood pal and amp builder Tony Mass were a small but steadfast part of preserving these sounds, holding down their Leyton corner of London, where they would pass the torch to Eljay Mass and an extant network of rigs, engineers, Deejays and ravers who really do it for the culture.

French club music sculptor (Marine) Benabou comes into her own on a handful of rolling pressure systems backed with Kliche’s dub-diffused breakbeat remix.

Slotting very neatly into Blank Mind’s roster of sparing dance engineers - Lina Filipovich, Paperclip Minimiser, DJ ojo - the Berlin-based producer brings her background as mastering/cutting engineer at ManMade to the fore on a rangy EP. The precision-tooled, syncopated percussion and stereo-strafe grayscale movement of opener ‘Projet G’ establishes parameters where she moves freely into vaporised dub techno (‘Interlude’), to something approaching Sandwell District gone samba in ‘Rise’, and restless forms of sinuous, sidewinding suss in ’Shift’, while ‘Merge’ demonstrates her feel for lucid, resonant clarity and depth perception. Label mate Kliche flexes ‘Projet G’ in a dubbier antechamber style in step with DJ ojo aces.

Co-produced by Nosaj Thing and 'Donnie Darko' OST guy Michael Andrews, Eartheater's latest is the polar opposite of 2023's 'Powders', ditching the drug and club references and leaning into baby-on-board playlist fodder, including an Oklou feature. RIYL Dido, Dubstar, Sneaker Pimps.

It's still obviously an Eartheater record, more 'Phoenix' than 'Powders'. The album starts strong, with her robotically treated voice sounding oddly soothing next to a full orchestra on 'Eyes of a Dove'. Even the glossy, sync-ready 'Paradise Rains', the album's first single that details her buying back her childhood farm and conceiving her baby, is chewably eccentric, still bound to the same logic that made her bonkers early material so addictive.

items.body:
London-based Malaysian-Australian composer and professor Silvia Lim prioritises close listening on 'Flare', writing quiet, minimal patterns that draw attention to unusual textures and bewitching dissonances.

Having bounced between Malaysia, Australia and the UK growing up, Lim is fascinated by the idea of instability and how that might be represented sonically. She explores a certain kind of fragility on 'Flare', working with the flimsiness of timbre by zooming in to capture the most incidental sounds - the scraping of a slowly pulled bow on the strings or the softness of air blown through a bass clarinet's reed. On the two-part composition 'Grafting', Lim folds in unexpectedly beautiful melodies, letting them grind to a halt completely, or disappear into faint traces beneath resonant ghost notes and stifled wails. There's a trace of folk music in there, buried in the undergrowth. 

And on the four-part 'Field of Play', Lim prepares her instruments with a single tool each time: a hair clip, a bobby pin and piece of cork, presenting the pieces as proof of what sonic shifts these seemingly light preparations might cause. On 'contact', the bobby pin disintegrates the instrumentation, turning the strings into lightly boiling, echoing resonances and on 'hidden place', it's even more disorienting, sounding as if the cello is being lowered slowly into a vast metallic chamber.

items.body:
5 Gate Temple’s high priest John T. Gast turns in 13 mystic trodders and pulse meditations on his first album, proper, dedicated to this style since 2019. Proper fantasy free party x soundsystem tekkerz, for transcendent club pressure.

As torch carrier of a mutant ’90s rave spirit since the early 2010’s, John T. Gast has opened up the cruddiest wormhole between formative Cornish raves and community centre dances. On ‘Infant’ he goes head down, feet first in a particularly briny, rinsed-out style of steppers livicating the enduring geists of early AFX and turbo-charged Jah Shaka with X-amount of moist noise and mystery in the air - the sort of stuff that feels like coming up at the blue hour in a smoke-choked warehouse or damp UK field, mud up to your shins, and loving it.

While it’s his first album since ‘SINEAD MEMORY TAPE’ in ’23, ‘Infant’ is his most substantial salvo in this signature steppers style since at least ‘5GTOUR’ (2019), or even ‘INNA BABALON’ (2016). Satisfyingly crusted with distortion around the edges and fully marshy underfoot, it best portrays the JTG essence in long form, conjuring an hour of heavily hypnotic atmospheres and fritzed production styles practically incomparable to anyone beyond his immediate family of 5GT label oddballs: Tribe of Colin, Xterea, YL Hooi, et al.

Hewing tighter than ever to his thing, JTG generates one of the baddest tools in his bag between the cloven-hoofed whirligig ‘7thfloor (Myrda Mix)’ and the air-stepping gait of ‘Population’, taking in his stride a sort of Kongo Tekno hunch on ‘Going In’ and byzantine ambience of ‘Mrzy 2 (Stone Mix)’,  making room for strains of zoned-out dankness before reeling back to the blunted ends of Caustic Window and the ribboning melodica and jabbing subs of ‘Rising’, before the astro junkyard pound of the title tune and the body-levitating mastery of ‘Goin In (Mer Mix)’.

It all leaves a peculiar tang.

Big tip!

items.body:
A leading light of neo-ambient takes their maiden bow on Glasgow’s stealthily expansive co:clear label after cherished turns with the sferic and Stroom labels.

The International Billionaire’s Love Child, or tiblsc for brevity, is the avatar of a Leipzig-based artist in possession of a distinctive, world-building ambient purview that has clearly stroked a nerve for listeners chasing the modern ambient zeitgeist, especially their couplet of ‘Delusive Tongue Shifts - Situation Based Compositions’ (2021) + ‘Hypertranslucent’ (2022). Those albums’ careful bends of pulpy sentiment and intricate, immersively dreamlike architecture is now echoed in ‘City of Something’, where her tender feel for compression and blends of HD and lo-fi tones fosters a gauzy sense of depth perception and sonorous emotional resonance. 

More so than her previous work, the eight tracks here are laced with a flickering pop spirit that riddles the album’s finely meshed dimensions, calling to mind aspects of Perila that are whisked to its most elegant frisson in ‘Resting Bitch Face’, or catching breathy contrails of an airspun pop song in ‘The Sun Really Is Something Round’, whilst tickling private parts of the imagination with the compressed artefacts of ‘You Just Want’, edging on Shinetiac’s take on smudged sheogaze trip hop in ‘Scare Me’, and teasing the most elusive urges on a secretive, quietly restive closer ‘Until the End of Time’.

In their sublime duo debut the simpatico synth & guitar of Jonny Nash & Tomo Katsurada is seduces to blissed, wind-whispering soundscapes, hashed out over the course of 12 months since Katsurada lent strings to Nash’s ‘Once Was Our Forever’. Dream material FFO Yuta Matsumura, Tenniscoats, Durutti Column...

"Netherlands-based artists Tomo Katsurada (Ex-Kikagaku Moyo / Future Days Radio) and Jonny Nash (Melody As Truth) combine forces for an exploration into the sonic potential of the guitar duo, rooted in their experiences performing together over the last 12 months.

Friends and admirers of each other’s work for a decade, their musical collaboration began in 2024 with Katsurada asking Nash to contribute guitar to his debut EP ‘Dream Of The Egg’. Sensing the need to explore this further, they spent the following year performing together in different configurations, with Nash joining Katsurada’s trio and Katsurada in turn playing with Nash as a duo, across a wide spectrum of spaces, from churches and temples to concert halls, theatres and outdoor festivals. With new ideas developing organically out of these performances, recording new material became the next logical step. A short period of three days was set aside with a clear goal: to capture the essence of their fluid, intertwining melodies and guitar playing in a way that felt as direct and unfiltered as possible. Working from a handful of pre-existing sketches, they left ample room for experimentation to unfold within the process.

The results are presented on ‘At The Emerald Pool’, a collection of ten pieces that offer the listener a full immersion into the pair’s sound. With guitar as the primary instrument for both artists, it is no surprise that the core of the album lies here, specifically in the fluid interplay between the two players. Layers of gentle, delay-soaked fingerpicking often make it almost impossible to distinguish where one player ends and the other begins. As soloists, both Katsurada and Nash have a gift for crafting melodic lines that feel open and ascending, expressive and hopeful without becoming saccharine. Longer, more abstract pieces are counterbalanced by a series of shorter songs, with five vocal tracks appearing across the album. The decision to share vocal duties lends the record a unique quality and a strong sense of variation, bringing a wide expressive range out of a deliberately focused musical framework.

‘At The Emerald Pool’ represents the first chapter in an ongoing musical dialogue, an attempt to capture a moment of connection, openness and discovery, laying the foundation for what continues to unfold."

items.body:
One of the most distinctive and legendary vocal/dub albums of all time, recorded in 1981 by the “dub dentist” Keith Hudson, ‘Playing It Cool & Playing It Right’ is now back in circulation for the first time in over 20 years, when it was first given overdue flowers via Basic Channel And Honest Jon’s ‘Basic Replay’ programme. It still burns with a rare energy, making it an untouchable, foundational text for the ages.

Keith Hudson (1946-1984) was one of dub reggae’s most distinctive innovators, renowned for a run of classic solo albums and productions for U-Roy, Big Youth, Ken Boothe and Horace Andy between 1972 and his untimely passing in 1984. However, Hudson's late period is where the real imperial juice can be found, a time that saw him move from Jamaican to London and New York studios, applying his unfathomable production style to a heavily americanised strain of vocal Soul. ‘Playing It Cool & Playing It Right’ is the pinnacle of that late period, an album that builds layer upon layer of alchemical brilliance.

Hudson’s combination of hooks and complex, highly unusual production is really unlike anything else from the period, or since, crooning in a soul mode made more haunting by a discreetly judicious application of tape FX, endlessly heavy subs, and mixing desk tricks deployed to delirious, almost psycho-acoustic effect.  The album was originally meant to feature one of Hudson's teenage sons to voice the dubs, but in the event the Love Joys, Wayne Jarrett, and inimitably Hudson himself featured at the microphone, with the dozen cuts co-produced by Wackies founder Lloyd ‘Bullwackie’ Barnes - the only collaboration between the two producers. It was originally issued on Hudson’s own label, Joint International, with subsequent pressings on Basic Replay in 2003, making it increasingly sought-after in the years since. 

Alongside reggae’s first concept album, ‘Flesh of My Skin, Blood of My Blood’, ‘Playing It Cool’ remains one the genre’s most important and unusual releases, picking up new disciples with every new wave of listeners taken aback by its stark, brooding blooze and brittle, spectral rendering.

The Sultans of Sludge slang a definitive label debut for Sub Pop, bringing their singular sound to roost on a legendary label local to their origins in the US north west, whose rugged landscapes fed directly into the LP’s formidably primal concentration of dualistic energies

Hailing some 30 years since Sunn O)))’s formation, their eponymous 10th studio album reckons with forces of nature - time and space, dark and light - for 80 minutes of air-shuddering pressure limning epic, craggy vistas from a thick haar of distortion. Subtly enlivened with field recordings made in forests near Bear Creek Studios, Woodinville, Washington, where O’Malley says they would “go hiking and be out in the woods, spend time outdoors”, the resulting six-part sequence sees the duo drill down to fundamentals with an absorbing sense of purpose and telepathically-attuned intuition. A notable dearth of other contributors also means it’s one of their truest statements as a duo; just Stephen O’Malley & Greg Anderson howling into the wilds on all instrumentation, from trusted axes to keys and electro-acoustic sorcery. 

At this point, not to labour the arboreal metaphors, but it may take a certified guide to see the wood for the trees in Sunn O))) lands, such is the uniquely coherent sprawl of their sound at 30 years up to the hilt in atonal rock doom. Our hair’s not long enough to lay claim as spirit guides, but after 23 years of bearing witness to them live, and ingesting most of their LPs, we can say this side is wholly emblematic of their radical steez. Between the two 18 minute totems of a ‘XXANN’ laced with location recording of running water at tender points, and a ‘Mindrolling’ monstered with claw-handed riffs, they take it to typically stare-down levels of intensity with the sustained threat of ‘Does Anyone Hear Like Venom?’, and billowing sheets of subharmonic distortion harnessed in ‘Everett Moses’. Closer ‘Glory Black’ is, however, a sort of sore thumb with a relatively conventional riff progression and rising banks of silvery wheeze that collapse into keys and field recordings, hearkening most closely to the duo’s precedents and NW peers in the Sub Pop roster, Earth, or even another touchstone, Black Sabbath, at their most strung out. 

Heavy as your life.

items.body:
Produced by Neek and Jabu's Amos Childs (aka O$VMV$M), Manonmars' third album is syrupy suite of smoke-hazed recollections and free associated reflections set to decelerated bumps, sluggish samples and cloudy drones = sturdy biz FFO Young Echo, Massive Attack, Cold Light, Ka, MIKE, King Vision Ultra, Coby Sey.

Manonmars' 2018 debut is one of those albums we still go back to periodically. It's that rare meeting of minds: a space for O$VMV$M to flex their production muscle and a scratchpad for London-based MC, painter and photographer Jack Martyn Richardson to sketch out a distinct vision of England. And His experiences and impressions on 'Entertainment System' still feel chewable. "Goddess on my arm and both our phones got no service," he quips on 'Goddess'. "Acid is lysergic, psychedelic rock is Turkish." His rhymes aren't throwaway, they map out an underground that's very recognisable, shadowed by O$VMV$M's tuff, effective soundscapes - beats that reference trip-hop, ambient music, exotica and '70s movie soundtracks as much as they do US rap. 

On opener 'Flam3throw3r', Mars raps in double-time over shrill horns that blot out any trace of a beat; Neek and Childs sound as if they relish the negative space, adding chic sword swipes to a track that's got little else to do with the Wu Tang Clan. When a lumbering beat kicks in on 'Decathlon', flipping from downtempo to no-tempo in the final act, it sounds as if it's just there to assert O$VMV$M's commitment to slowness - Mars doesn't even seem to notice, rhyming casually but never losing his flow.

Bristol mainstays Franco Franco and Dali de Saint Paul turn up to assist on 'Volcanic Shield', one of the album's most conventional bangers, led by O$VMV$M's skittering Surf Gang-like beats and morse code blips, and cold light's Birthmark lends his voice to 'Infinite', going bar for bar with Mars over Neek and Childs' slackened funk, blaring out like an old tape on a busted in-car audio system. 'Firewater' takes the same approach, leaving Mars to do his best as snares splash across the spectrum with added sax from Brum-based sound artist Lorenzo Prati. "My bitch white, she can scuba dive and ice climb," he spits. "Put the drink down, I wasn't in my right mind." 

It's music that laughs through the tears - what could be more British than that?

Cold Spring re-issue 'Offal' by industrial pioneers Sutcliffe Jugend (ex WHITEHOUSE).

"Sutcliffe Jugend take everything to a new level with the beautifully packaged album Offal. With printed lyrics included for the first time, we get to the heart of Sutcliffe Jugend at their euphoric and vilifying best. Words that will make you question what it is to be truly human and not the conformist PC neo-liberal slave so prevalent and encouraged in the modern era.

The production on the album sounds massive compared to previous releases, giving the carefully constructed songs an intense, brutal and relentless environment not heard before. Kevin Tomkins' vocals are pushed to new extremes, doing battle with Paul Taylor's vicious guitar and synth work. 

Offal features four epic tracks (55 minutes) of naked emotional release that will leave the listener breathless and gasping for more."

Gathering the short-lived Boston emo outfit's influential debut 'Junk', shoegaze-y sophomore album 'This Afternoon Malady', the unfinished third album and everything in-between, 'Wait A Lifetime' will be crucial listening if you're more than a casual Jejune fan.

Jejune were never the Berklee-educated New England scene's best band, but they proved their mettle all the same, penning a pair of albums that almost inadvertently steered the course of the emo underground. Those records aren't without their faults, sure, but it's hard to get an accurate read on the US scene without them. And they've never sounded better; with a fresh lick of paint, 'Junk' and its superior, if way more misunderstood follow-up deserves to be filed alongside Karate's early records at the very least. And for the heads, 'Wait A Lifetime' sweeps up all the band's recorded material, the loose singles, split EPs and compilation tracks, even excavating the sessions from their aborted third album and commissioning an essay from critic Nina Corcoran to fill in the gaps.

Sandwell District’s Dave Sumner aka Function completes his Existenz cycle for Tresor with an expansive, full spectrum strafe from beat-less ambient to slow acid, electro and signature deep techno gems.

Seven years since his ‘Existenz’ album for Tresor, and leading on from related EPs for Rrose’s Eaux and his own Infrastructure New York, Sumner reflects on what prompted his LP, and interim strife, across six tracks tallying to an LP in their own right. After immersion in his patented style of nocturnal pads and lustrous acid lines, it shouldn’t be hard to identify his touch on some of Sandwell District’s most romantic high points, finely-sculpted in a style that has served him damn well since the mid-late ‘90s origins of NYC & Brum techno.

Shine-eyed reflections of early ‘90s electronica radiate from opener ‘Ascent’ into 12 mins of sleekly heady, decelerated acid house less on ‘City of Luz’, and what could almost be an SD cut in the mouth-watering detailing and elegant drive of ‘Transmutation’. He continues to hanker for lushness in the club on the whirring, melancholic offbeat propulsion to another standout, ‘Growth Cycle (Hermetic Mix)’, before turning darker with flashes of Kraftwerk-via-his NYC electro touchstones on ‘November 29’, and deferred gratification of ‘Rubedo’.

Resounding macro noise tumult and doom drone wrangling by a bastion of the US scene, dong it for one of its consistently intriguing labels, fostering one side of tremulous, ringing atonalities and sustained, nails-on-blackboard menace that buckles under the intensity, while dialling down the higher register squall to a treacly drone and and bubbling ructions on the other side.

“To a polite society, things such as chaos, noise, and anarchy threaten the normative structures that can assert control and maintain power over others. New York noise icon Bob Bellerue qualifies his practice as a form of sonic animism, in which engages with that which is unheard in materials, equipment, and their relationships, developing a process of amplified discovery. The unhinged, the unquantifiable, and the unknowable are all possible outcomes in Bellerue's expansive works. In Bellerue's words, "The universe is a feedback loop. Creating and destroying. Growing and decaying. Loving and dying. Expanding and contracting. The big bang is the end result of everything merging together in the biggest black hole ever and then erupting into being over and over again. Praise chaos!””

The key members of Animal Collective & Spacemen 3 yield a sumptuous 2nd duo LP of ‘60s Beach Boys harmonies via garage-psych-dub-pop and tied off with a ribbon-bow of lysergic studio sorcery, everything soft and glowing to the touch. Happy days...

"It is built on loops of harp (Mary Lattimore) and sequences of steel drum, webs of pedal steel and even bits of a mariachi band. These are, of course, deliberate choices, sounds and textures they’ve never used and that offered a clear sonic break from the success of Reset. But maybe more than ever, Sonic Boom and Panda Bear emerge through these 10 songs as two people with frank opinions about these times, with a real stake in the sway of the world. These tunes grapple with online exhaustion and pervasive depression, with political chicanery and ecological sustainability, all while advocating for respecting the power of luck and giving one another grace in a moment when very few of us actually know what the hell is happening.

Has it ever been easier to complain publicly about something without trying to change it? Sonic Boom and Panda Bear are not content to gripe about circumstances or speculate about the fall on A ? of WHEN. The goal is for the music to create physical connections between people, to encourage them to enjoy a real experience in the world with it and each other."

items.body:
Thee darkest, weirdest dub perennial from Keith Hudson, 1979, blooms on vinyl for first time in years, ready to scatter smoke and minds into the late and early hours...

First released in 1979 and highly in-demand ever since, the dub sibling to Keith Hudson’s ‘Nuh Skin Up’ pushes that album’s already stark blooz and The Soul Syndicate’s deadly riddims hard into the echo chamber with a balance of experimental nous and heads-down grooves that has assured its place in the pantheon of the most haunting dubs. 

Out of print for decades until a 2007 pressing spiked it back in the water table, the album firmly holds up nearly a half century since its original release on the basis of a future proofed minimalism that continues to haunt successive generations with its bony percussion and a dematerialised soul exemplary of dub metaphysics at its transcendant best.

Up there with the likes of Lee ‘Scratch’ Perry in terms of his dual role as songwriter and desk-tweaking dub maverick, Hudson really gets inside his own tunes, and The Soul Syndicate’s instrumentals, with the uncanniest insight, turning the likes of its title corker into clouds of pillowy steppers bass and streaking echoic contrails.

The way he inverts the vocals on ‘Ire Ire’ to sound properly wrong-end-of-telescope against the foregrounded crack of congas and spectral organ is just magic, and lays the groundwork for so much dub experimentation to come from the likes of everyone from Rhythm & Sound to Tricky, along with the likes of his spellbinding, skeletal steppers dub masterwork ‘Troubles’.

100% killer reissue of Bim Sherman’s self-released 1988 dub masterpiece ‘Ghetto Dub’, mixed by King Tubby, Prince Jammy and Adrian Sherwood who diffuse rhythms by The Roots Radics and Sly & Robbie, newly remastered for its first new edition in 30 years.

With 2nd hand prices understandably climbing into triple figures, this overdue first vinyl reissue will be mana to the fiends. It takes pride of place in an ongoing programme of resurrected Sherman aces to portray him at his most elusive and atmospheric, or as the hype sticker calls it, “a journey in echo and space”.

His legendarily tone is threaded thru the desk by a team of JA/UK titans with the man himself in the producer role, sifting cuts from his Century Records: a label set up in the Uk in 1984, after his move from Kingston, JA, to London, where he became a crucial figure in the On-U Sound crew after joining their 1979 tour, and would lend to classic Dub Syndicate cuts among others. 

The record’s renown has grown over the years since Sherman’s passing in 2000 and the effective dissolution of his label. Week-End Records now do a sterling job of preserving his legacy with this edition, richly representing the warmth and pressure of the OG in its entirety, from the clean-spurred, buoyant step of its title tune to moon-booted ‘Untitled Dub’, via the soul-tugging ace ’Station Dub’ with its unanswered doorbells, and best showcase of his voice in ‘Moving Dub’, another alright stepper in ‘World Dub’, the bloozy wooze of ‘Danger Dub’ and wickedly skewed Afro-lilt of ‘Tribulation Dub.’

All killer.

At the age of 72, "Evil" Graham Lee, the legendary pedal steel pioneer and veteran of the iconic Australian band The Triffids, delivers his first ever album under his own name titled ‘I Think I’m Alone Now’.

"In addition to his work with The Triffids, Graham’s place in ambient history was cemented in 1990 when his evocative pedal steel became the soulful centerpiece of The KLF’s masterpiece, Chill Out (specifically on the highlight “Baltimore to Fair Play”).

I Think I’m Alone Now is a profound exploration of the instrument's emotional range, blending traditional country infused melodies with vast, reverb drenched ambient textures. The album spans six tracks, anchored by the Side B title track, a 15 minute textural piece that leans heavily into the ambient genre. From the delicate melancholy of "Seeking Beauty in Sadness" to the curious abstraction of "Nursery in the Beehive," Lee uses his pedal steel and an array of pedals to sculpt unique, haunting soundscapes that exist between tradition and the avant garde.

The connection is brought full circle with exclusive liner notes written by The KLF’s Bill Drummond. Reflecting on a forty year friendship that began when The Triffids served as the backing band for Drummond’s solo debut, The Man, Drummond provides a personal and poignant context for this long awaited solo bow."
